keyTerms.definition: A price or spec table tied to one verification date.
Choices like start cheap, measure on evals, and cache static prefixes.

recall.answer: Treat every price table as a dated snapshot. The decision patterns do not change when prices do.
recall.question: How should you treat the price tables in this volume?

sections.title: D2: Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

keyTerms.definition: A chunk of text the model reads and writes, roughly four characters.
Everything sent in one request: system instructions, messages, tools, documents.
A system trained to predict the next token, over and over.
A request with no memory: you re-send history and pay for the whole prompt.

recall.answer: The system instructions, the conversation messages, the tool definitions, and any retrieved documents. It is the model's entire world for that request.
recall.question: What is a prompt made of?

recall.answer: A large language model predicts the next token repeatedly until the answer is complete. A token is a chunk of text, roughly three to four characters of English.
recall.question: Define a token and a language model in one sentence each.

recall.answer: You re-send history, you pay for the whole prompt, and nothing outside the prompt exists for the model.
recall.question: Why does a follow-up message 'forget' earlier context?

sections.title: Unit 1. What a prompt is and how Claude reads it

keyTerms.definition: The four Claude models, each tuned for a different job and price.
The total tokens the model can consider in one request.
Per million tokens: the unit for model prices.
Tokens the model writes; they cost five times input tokens on every model.

recall.answer: Haiku fits high-volume simple work. Sonnet is the everyday default. Opus fits sustained agentic coding. Fable fits the hardest reasoning.
recall.question: Name the four tiers and the job each is built for.

recall.answer: Output tokens cost exactly five times input tokens on every model. Anything that makes the model write more pays the 5x rate.
recall.question: What is the output-to-input price ratio?

recall.answer: Test Haiku or Sonnet against the bar first. The credited answer is the tier whose measured quality clears the bar at the lowest cost and latency.
recall.question: A triage bot on Opus hits 94% against a 90% requirement. What next?

sections.title: Unit 2. The Claude model family: who is who

keyTerms.definition: Asking directly with no examples.
Showing input-output examples first so the model copies the pattern.
Asking the model to reason step by step before answering.
Built-in reasoning controlled by an effort or budget setting.

recall.answer: Zero-shot asks directly with no examples. Few-shot shows examples first. Chain-of-thought asks for step-by-step reasoning. Move right only when difficulty demands it.
recall.question: What are the three prompting techniques, in order of cost?

recall.answer: CoT generates reasoning as output tokens, and output costs 5x input. On tasks where zero-shot already works, CoT adds cost and latency for no quality gain.
recall.question: Why is chain-of-thought the costliest technique?

recall.answer: Drop CoT and verify with the eval. The cost comes from output tokens that caching cannot discount, and accuracy is unchanged.
recall.question: Extraction runs 99.1% with or without CoT, but the bill tripled. What is the credited move?

keyTerms.definition: Standing instructions sent with every request, before the conversation.
A system prompt with slots filled in per request or deployment.
Behavioral rules written in the prompt: refuse, escalate, validate shape.
The dedicated request field carrying standing orders, separate from messages.

recall.answer: Without one you paste the same instructions into every user message, which is error-prone, wasteful, and hard to cache. A system prompt centralizes the constants in one versioned place.
recall.question: Why not just paste instructions into every user message?

recall.answer: A slot that changes per request changes the prompt prefix and can silently kill the cache hit rate. Put volatile slots at the end.
recall.question: Where do volatile template slots go, and why?

recall.answer: A prompt instruction is not a security control. Prompt injection can argue with guardrails, so real safety boundaries need system-level controls outside the prompt.
recall.question: Where do prompt guardrails stop being enough?

sections.title: Unit 4. System prompts: the constitution of your application

keyTerms.definition: The total tokens the model can consider in one request, input plus output.
Spare window capacity kept so a session survives growth.
Summarizing old turns so a long conversation keeps working.
The token cap on what the model may write in one request.

recall.answer: 600,000 history plus 128,000 max output is 728,000, inside 1,000,000. Adding 400,000 retrieved tokens pushes it to 1,128,000, which fails.
recall.question: Does 600K of history plus 128K max output fit a 1M window? What breaks it?

recall.answer: Each turn's input plus output becomes the next turn's input. Tool results, retrieved documents, and examples stack up fast.
recall.question: Why does turn 20 cost more than turn 1?

recall.answer: Compact old turns and prune tool results. The problem is unbounded history growth, not the window size.
recall.question: A coding agent slows down and forgets early instructions by turn 30. What is the credited fix?

sections.title: Unit 5. Context window management: budget it like money

keyTerms.definition: Reusing work the API already did on an identical prompt prefix.
The identical start of the prompt that caching can reuse.
The marked point in the prompt where caching starts.
How long a cache entry lives: 5 minutes or 1 hour.
The share of requests served from cache instead of recomputed.

recall.answer: When the prompt prefix is identical to a recent request, the model skips reprocessing it. You pay a small fraction of the input price, cutting input spend 70 to 90 percent.
recall.question: How does prompt caching work?

recall.answer: Move the breakpoint to the end of the static prefix, before the session ID. The changing session ID poisons the prefix hash on every request.
recall.question: A cached prompt has a 2% hit rate with a breakpoint after a per-request session ID. What is the fix?

recall.answer: 512 tokens for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, 1,024 for Sonnet 5, and 4,096 for Haiku 4.5. Shorter prompts silently skip caching.
recall.question: What are the minimum cacheable lengths per model?

sections.title: Unit 6. Prompt caching: the cheapest big lever

keyTerms.definition: Instructions broken into small versioned pieces composed per task.
A packaged unit of expertise: a SKILL.md plus scripts and resources.
The file carrying a Skill's name, description, and instructions.
One giant prompt doing everything: unmaintainable and taxed every request.

recall.answer: Five copies of the same instructions become five slightly different instructions within a quarter, and nobody knows which one is canonical.
recall.question: Why do copy-paste prompts rot?

recall.answer: A tool is a function the model can call; it does something. A Skill packages knowledge about how to do something well.
recall.question: Skill versus tool?

recall.answer: Extract the shared instructions into versioned modules or a Skill, and place the stable shared content at the front so it forms a cacheable prefix.
recall.question: Twelve agents share compliance instructions via copy-paste. What is the credited pair?

sections.title: Unit 7. Prompt reuse: modular prompts and Skills

keyTerms.definition: Start at Haiku, climb only on measured failure, stop when a tier passes.
Latency and cost limits that can disqualify a model that passes quality.
Settings letting a model spend more compute thinking before answering.
The maximum the solution may spend: the binding constraint in batch jobs.

recall.answer: Rank candidates by cost and speed, start at Haiku, climb only when measurements say the cheaper tier fails, and stop the moment a tier passes.
recall.question: State the selection framework.

recall.answer: An extra $31,500 every month for one million turns, for nothing. Cost gaps between tiers are multiples, not percentages.
recall.question: If Haiku clears the quality bar, what does choosing Fable cost?

recall.answer: Test Haiku on the summarization eval. No latency constraint forces a faster tier, and the cost ceiling is the binding constraint.
recall.question: An overnight batch job has a $2,000 budget; the Sonnet prototype costs $4,800. What now?

sections.title: Unit 8. The selection framework: the cheapest model that passes

keyTerms.definition: Start at Haiku, climb only on measured failure, stop when a tier passes.
Pinning the cache start at the end of the static prefix.

recall.answer: The selection framework says to check the cheaper tier before committing. Haiku at 3M requests a month could roughly halve the bill.
recall.question: Sonnet prototype passes every constraint. Why is D still the answer?

recall.answer: Pin an explicit breakpoint at the end of the static prefix, and move the volatile customer record after it.
recall.question: Automatic caching never hits on a prompt with a changing customer record. What are the two fixes?
